answer.label: Not Pythagoras — a modern paraphrase of Ovid
answer.sourceLine: No writing by Pythagoras survives. The idea comes from the speech Ovid gives him in Metamorphoses XV: whoever cuts a calf’s throat is “prepar[ing] himself for shedding human blood.” None of these sentences is in that speech, though. The earliest source Wikiquote cites for this wording is Jon Wynne-Tyson’s The Extended Circle (1985).

source.heading: The closest real text

docMeta.dd: Ovid (completed by AD 8), in a speech he gives to Pythagoras
Henry T. Riley, 1851 prose translation (Project Gutenberg eBook #26073)

source.excerpt: How greatly he disgraces himself, how in his impiety does he prepare himself for shedding human blood, who cuts the throat of the calf with the knife, and gives a deaf ear to its lowings! or who can kill the kid as it sends forth cries like those of a child; or who can feed upon the bird to which he himself has given food. How much is there wanting in these instances for downright criminality? A {short} step {only} is there thence {to it}!
trail: Wikiquote’s Pythagoras page ↗ gives the full three-sentence line as an “Attribution to Pythagoras by Ovid.” Its only sources are modern: Jon Wynne-Tyson’s The Extended Circle: A Dictionary of Humane Thought (1985), p. 260, and Vegetarian Times No. 168 (August 1991), p. 4.
Wynne-Tyson’s anthology was published in 1985 by Centaur (Internet Archive record ↗). The scan is lending-only, so we could not read page 260 to see what source, if any, it gives.

We checked the speech of Pythagoras in Ovid’s Metamorphoses XV in Riley’s 1851 translation ↗. It has “dainties without slaughter and bloodshed” and “one living creature to exist through the death of another living creature.” It does not have the popular sentences.

In Ovid’s Latin ↗, the nearest lines are XV.463–465: “quam male consuescit, quem se parat ille cruori / inpius humano, vituli qui guttura ferro / rumpit.” That is about preparing oneself for human bloodshed. It says nothing of “health or peace” or “joy and love.”
source.cutTag: Ovid's real lines, not the popular quote
source.excerptNote: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV.463–465, in Henry T. Riley’s 1851 translation; the braces are Riley’s. Ovid’s argument, that killing animals leads to killing people, is the seed of the modern quote. But “ruthless destroyer of lower living beings,” “massacre animals,” “kill each other” and “seed of murder and pain” appear nowhere in the speech.

source.rightsNote: The popular English wording has no identifiable author or first publication: the earliest source Wikiquote cites is a 1985 anthology, which we could not read. So we make no rights claim for it. Ovid’s Latin and Henry T. Riley’s 1851 translation (quoted above) are in the public domain, but neither contains this wording.

author.name: Ovid
author.heading: About Ovid
author.metaLine: 43 BC – AD 17/18 · Roman poet, author of the Metamorphoses
author.bio: Publius Ovidius Naso had finished his mythological epic, the Metamorphoses, by AD 8. Its final book opens with a long speech by Pythagoras that urges people to stop eating meat. In that speech Ovid argues that a man who kills a calf or a kid is training himself to shed human blood. That is the real seed of this modern quote, but Ovid never wrote the sentences that circulate today.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Pythagoras
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely shared “Pythagoras” lines on vegetarian and animal-rights sites. It borrows real authority: Ovid made Pythagoras the voice of a famous anti-meat sermon. But the wording is modern.

items.why: “No authentic writings of Pythagoras have survived,” notes Wikipedia ↗. Every saying credited to him comes through later writers, and none of them has been shown to contain this one.
Ovid’s Pythagoras does argue that a man who cuts a calf’s throat “prepare[s] himself for shedding human blood” (Riley translation ↗). The three popular sentences are not in the speech.
Wikiquote ↗ sources the line only to Jon Wynne-Tyson’s The Extended Circle (1985) and Vegetarian Times (August 1991), with no ancient citation.

misattribution.truthLine: This is a modern paraphrase in Pythagoras’s name. It loosely echoes Ovid’s Metamorphoses XV.463–465 (Latin text ↗), but no ancient author is known to have written these sentences.

context.heading: Why the line sounds ancient
lead: Ovid’s Metamorphoses, finished by AD 8, ends with a long lecture by Pythagoras against eating animals. As Wikipedia ↗ notes, “his teachings as portrayed in Ovid’s Metamorphoses would later influence the modern vegetarian movement.” That is why modern vegetarian writing so often quotes him.

Over time, anthologies and magazines turned Ovid’s argument into tidier, modern-sounding sayings. This one even serves as the caption of Rubens’s painting Pythagoras Advocating Vegetarianism on Wikiquote ↗. The idea is old, but these words are not.
context.pull: A short step only is there thence to it.
